title: config.toml is the sole trust root and is consumed by a bare read with no ownership, permission, or reparse-point check, while the only confinement helper in the tree is compiled out on the primary platform
description: The entire no-trust-on-first-use guarantee is implemented in Config::from_toml: a key enters the registry only because the operator wrote it into config.toml (a missing pubkey is a fatal load failure at acl/lib.rs:175-183), and Board::dispatch then verifies every message against that key (idboardd/src/lib.rs:105 then :116). Config::load performs that step as an unconditional std::fs::read_to_string of whatever bytes sit at an env- or flag-derived path (acl/lib.rs:252, reached from idboardd/src/main.rs:67 and :71, and from wrapper.rs:183). It never checks the file's owner, permissions or DACL, never rejects a symlink or reparse point, never canonicalises the path, and never verifies an integrity digest. The state root is created by Store::open through layout::ensure_dir, the bare create_dir_all (store/lib.rs:115), not ensure_private_dir; and ensure_private_dir, the only helper that would restrict a directory, sets a mode solely under #[cfg(unix)] (layout.rs:169-173) and compiles to `let _ = dir;` on Windows (layout.rs:174-177), which is the project's primary target. VERIFIED by the reviewer: a workspace-wide search for security_descriptor, set_dacl, dacl, set_permissions, from_mode, PermissionsExt, sddl and icacls returns exactly three hits, all #[cfg(unix)]: layout.rs:171-172 (0o700 on directories) and keystore.rs:161-165 and :252/:262 (0o600 on the key file). There is no Windows file-ACL code and no named-pipe security-descriptor code anywhere in the tree. So the custody of the file that decides who may be `lead` reduces on Windows to inherited NTFS ACLs that this code neither sets nor verifies; layout.rs:163-166 asserts in a comment that the inheritance is adequate, and that assertion is never enforced. A substituted key is also self-consistent: the fingerprint is derived from the parsed key at acl/lib.rs:207 rather than read from config, so the fingerprint cross-check at keys.rs:308-317 cannot detect it; the only signal is the rotation warning at idboardd/src/main.rs:86-93. Principal framing: README.md:42-49 places a same-user process inside the documented boundary and README.md:54 places root, SYSTEM and an administrator outside the threat model entirely, so the only in-scope principal is a second non-administrative local account. Whether the inherited DACL on that account's config.toml permits the write is a platform fact outside this repository's source, so the record is reported as needing validation rather than confirmed.
claimed_root_cause: The trust-root file is loaded by a single unconditional read that performs no ownership, permission, DACL, reparse-point or integrity check, and the one directory-confinement helper in the codebase is compiled out on the primary platform, so custody of the registry that decides every identity's signing key is asserted by a source comment (layout.rs:163-166) rather than established by code.

trace.scope: Config::load, invoked by idboardd/src/main.rs:71 with the path from args.config or layout::config_path (idboardd/src/main.rs:67), and by wrapper.rs:183 with opts.config_path. The path is selected by an environment variable (IDBOARD_CONFIG, layout.rs:71-76) or a command-line flag.
trace.description: The daemon's identity registry is loaded from a caller-selected path with no custody precondition on the file, no canonicalisation, and no check that the resolved object is a regular file rather than a link or reparse point.

trace.scope: Config::load body
trace.description: std::fs::read_to_string(path) with no ownership, permission, DACL, symlink or integrity check of any kind. Whatever bytes are present at that path become the trust root; the only later constraint is TOML syntax and shape, enforced at lines 156-244.

trace.scope: from_toml identity loop, identities.insert
trace.description: The parsed key becomes Identity.public_key and is published at line 208. fingerprint is derived from that same key at line 207 rather than read from config, so a substituted key is internally consistent and invisible to the fingerprint cross-check at keys.rs:308-317. Presence and parse failures at lines 169-191 are fatal, but they constrain only the file's syntax, never its provenance.

trace.scope: Board::dispatch, the key looked up at line 105 is passed to verify_with_key
trace.description: The key read from that file is the sole authority for the identity, and Board has no second source against which to cross-check it. Whoever controls the file's bytes controls which key each existing identity name maps to, and therefore full post and read authority on every channel that name may use under acl/lib.rs:100-111, plus the ability to deny the genuine agent, which surfaces only as the rotation warning at idboardd/src/main.rs:86-93.

evidence.description: std::fs::read_to_string(path) is the complete load step; there is no ownership, permission, DACL, symlink or integrity check between the filesystem and the registry.
identities.insert publishes the parsed key as Identity.public_key, the only verifying key; fingerprint is derived at line 207 so a substituted key cannot be detected by fingerprint mismatch.

The no-trust-on-first-use control itself: a missing pubkey is a fatal load failure and the error names the fix. This is a strong control on which names may exist, and it is entirely orthogonal to who wrote the file.

The #[cfg(not(unix))] arm of ensure_private_dir is `let _ = dir;`, so on the project's primary target the function is create_dir_all and nothing else; the 0o700 mode at line 172 never compiles on Windows.

The source asserts the deployment fact this candidate turns on, that NTFS inherits ACLs from %USERPROFILE% which already grant the creating user and SYSTEM and deny Everyone and that this is adequate, as a doc comment, with no code anywhere in the tree that sets or verifies it.

Store::open creates the state root with layout::ensure_dir, the unrestricted create_dir_all, so the directory holding config.toml and idboard.db is never given an explicit restrictive mode or DACL by this code. crates/idboard/src/lock.rs:60 is a second caller of the permissive helper.

config.identity(&env.sender_id) followed by verify_with_key(&identity.public_key, env) at line 116 is the entire authority decision; it trusts the loaded file completely and holds no second reference against which the key could be cross-checked.

The documented non-goal: a same-user process reading ~/.idboard/keys/ is out of scope, and README.md:54 puts root, SYSTEM and an administrator out of scope too. This is why the only in-scope principal for this candidate is a second non-administrative local account, and why the finding must be framed as custody of the trust root rather than as a same-user weakness.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox available on the audit host to execute the bounded local check

The effective DACL of the idboard state root and of config.toml on the target platform is not source-visible. layout.rs:174-177 compiles the only confinement helper out on Windows and no code path in the tree sets or verifies a file ACL or a named-pipe security descriptor, so whether a second non-administrative local account can create or modify the state root's config.toml cannot be determined from source. The custody assumption the finding turns on is asserted only in the comment at layout.rs:163-166.

validation_plan.local: On a throwaway Windows VM with two local accounts, as the owner: create the state root and a minimal config.toml with one [identity.probe] whose pubkey comes from `idboard keygen probe` run under the second account, then as the second account attempt to append a second [identity.probe] entry carrying its own pubkey, and separately to delete-and-replace the file. Record whether either write succeeds, then start idboardd and read the startup summary to see whether both pubkeys or only the substituted one took effect. Stop after reading the summary; do not exercise the substituted identity against a live board.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed read on the real host: run `icacls` against the state root and its config.toml and record the owner, the inheritance source, and every principal granted write or modify. Compare that against the list this code intends, which is the single owning account plus SYSTEM. If any other principal holds write, the candidate resolves in favour of the finding; if not, the finding closes as an inherited-ACL assumption that holds for this deployment and the residual is hardening only.

title: apply_timeouts discards ErrorKind::Unsupported and still reports success, so no socket in the tree is proven to carry an I/O deadline and the framing read has no time-based exit
description: Source shape, with the attribution and the impact scope corrected. apply_timeouts (ipc/lib.rs:181-194) calls set_recv_timeout and set_send_timeout at :183-184, discards ErrorKind::Unsupported in the empty arm at :189, and returns Ok(()) at :193. A function whose entire purpose is to install a deadline therefore reports success having installed none, and IO_TIMEOUT (ipc/lib.rs:51) is dead configuration on the platform the daemon is actually built for. Correction 1, misattribution in the original candidate title: read_frame_from (ipc/lib.rs:206-241) is generic over R: BufRead and is not where a deadline could ever be installed; it is the Stream handed to it by accept (:137), try_accept (:154) or connect (:166) that carries or lacks the deadline. The defect belongs to the Stream, not to the framing function. Correction 2, the decisive fact is not source-provable here: whether interprocess 2.4.4 returns ErrorKind::Unsupported for a Windows named pipe, which is dead configuration, or returns Ok with a real 10-second deadline in force, is library behaviour that does not exist in this repository. The only in-repo support for the Unsupported case is a doc comment at ipc/lib.rs:172-175, and the one test that touches the function, applying_timeouts_never_fails_on_either_platform at ipc/lib.rs:423-432, asserts only that the call is Ok, which is satisfied identically by Unsupported having been swallowed and by the deadline having actually been set. The suite therefore pins the swallow rather than any deadline, and no test anywhere releases a stalled reader. That unobservable is retained as a blocker rather than assumed. Correction 3, impact scope and non-double-counting: standalone, this is the already-documented residual at ipc/lib.rs:177-180 and README.md:326-329, namely that four stalled connections consume the fixed worker pool. The cross-identity outage is NOT this record's consequence; it belongs to idboardd.serve.board_mutex_held_across_peer_blocking_io, which consumes this precondition. The two are two records, not one: different files, different invariants, an absent deadline in the transport versus a lock held across peer-paced I/O in the daemon, and non-overlapping fixes. The genuine additional scope found in source, which the original candidate did not record, is the relay path: the same missing deadline is present per invocation, where wrapper.rs:367 and wrapper.rs:403 sit inside the wrapper's single relay serve loop, which is itself the supervise loop at wrapper.rs:350-378 that also polls child exit status at :356 and the interrupt flag at :351. One stalled child connection there blocks the wrapper's tick. On that path the affected principal is the SAME identity, so it is within-identity and not cross-tenant; the cross-identity blast radius comes only from the daemon.
claimed_root_cause: crates/idboard-ipc/src/lib.rs:189 discards ErrorKind::Unsupported from set_recv_timeout/set_send_timeout and still returns Ok(()) at :193, so the function reports success while installing no deadline on the accepted, polled or connected Stream, leaving the peer-paced read at ipc/lib.rs:210 and the write at :262 with no time-based termination on the primary platform.

trace.scope: any local process opening the daemon named pipe: unauthenticated, no token, no DACL, no key
trace.description: idboard_ipc::accept(&listener) is the daemon's only acquisition of a Stream and therefore the last point at which a deadline could be attached to the connection an unauthenticated peer controls.

trace.scope: accept, every daemon connection and every relay poll
trace.description: apply_timeouts(&stream) is invoked before the Stream is returned to the caller. The same call is made at ipc/lib.rs:154 by try_accept, which is what wrapper.rs:367 uses for the per-invocation relay, and at ipc/lib.rs:166 by connect, so this is the only place in the tree where a deadline could be installed for any socket.

trace.scope: ErrorKind::Unsupported, the expected Windows named-pipe result per the doc comment at :172
trace.description: The Unsupported arm is an empty block, so control falls through to return Ok(()) at :193 with nothing set. The same swallow applies to set_send_timeout at :184, so write_frame's write_all at :262 is deadline-free too; that write blocks only once a reply exceeds what the OS pipe buffer absorbs, so for the small pre-authentication responses it is a conditional path rather than the sink this record turns on.

trace.scope: daemon consumer of the un-deadlined Stream
trace.description: read_frame is called on the accepted Stream with whatever deadline apply_timeouts left in place. This is where the absent deadline becomes a held worker and, through the board mutex taken at main.rs:135, a cross-identity outage; that escalation is recorded under idboardd.serve.board_mutex_held_across_peer_blocking_io and is not claimed here.

trace.scope: relay consumer of the same un-deadlined Stream, same identity only
trace.description: The wrapper's read_frame runs inside the single relay serve loop, which is the supervise loop at wrapper.rs:350-378, so an un-deadlined stall there also stops child-status polling at :356 and interrupt handling at :351 for that invocation. The affected principal is the same identity, not a different one.

trace.scope: peer-controlled read with no proven deadline
trace.description: read_frame_from loops on reader.fill_buf() and returns only on a newline (:222-230), a clean EOF (:215-221) or an error (:213). MAX_FRAME_BYTES at :224 and :233 bounds accumulated bytes only once bytes arrive, so a peer that sends nothing, or a partial line under 1 MiB, never terminates the read. This is the operation the absent deadline leaves unbounded, and it is the same call the daemon performs at main.rs:177 and the wrapper at :403.

evidence.description: Err(ref e) if e.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::Unsupported => {} -- the root-cause line. The failure is swallowed and the function still reports success at :193, so the caller has no way to know a deadline is absent.

pub const IO_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10) -- the intended deadline, with the doc comment at :46-50 stating its purpose is to stop a client that connects and then goes quiet. If Unsupported is the real result, this constant is dead configuration on the primary platform.

The comment that Windows named pipes do not support these timeouts, that failing there would make the daemon unusable on its primary target, and that the code proceeds without a deadline instead. This comment is the ONLY in-repo support for the decisive fact; it is prose about a third-party library's behaviour, not code, and nothing in the tree verifies it.

if buf.len() + n > MAX_FRAME_BYTES { return Err(IpcError::FrameTooLarge); } -- the only bound in read_frame_from, and it is conditional on bytes arriving, so it does not bound a stalled reader. The same conditionality applies at :224.

fn applying_timeouts_never_fails_on_either_platform() -- asserts only that the call is Ok, with the comment at :421-422 saying Windows named pipes reject I/O timeouts. The assertion is satisfied both when Unsupported was swallowed and when a real 10 s deadline was installed, so the test cannot distinguish the two and pins the swallow rather than any deadline. No test anywhere releases a stalled reader or writer.

Err(e) => return Err(e.into()) -- the only propagating arm. For the unsupported-socket case it is never reached, so the one error path that could have surfaced the missing deadline to the caller is exactly the path the platform does not take.

The un-deadlined read is consumed here, and because the board lock is already held at main.rs:135 the missing deadline becomes a cross-identity outage. That consequence is recorded under idboardd.serve.board_mutex_held_across_peer_blocking_io, not here.

match idboard_ipc::try_accept(&listener) -- the relay path, which reaches apply_timeouts at ipc/lib.rs:154 and the identical deadline-free read at :403. This widens the affected surface beyond the daemon but keeps it within one identity per invocation.
The sibling-binary lookup hardcodes a .exe suffix, so the end-to-end suite only exercises the platform on which the Unsupported path is claimed, and no test anywhere drives a stalled peer.

The documented limitation that Windows named pipes have no equivalent of SO_RCVTIMEO for pipe handles and that interprocess reports Unsupported. A deliberate, documented limitation; the part that is not documented is the interaction with the daemon's single board mutex, which is the other record's finding.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox available on the audit host to execute the bounded local check; whether a stalled peer is actually released after IO_TIMEOUT is an observation, not a source fact

whether interprocess 2.4.4's set_recv_timeout and set_send_timeout on a Windows named pipe return ErrorKind::Unsupported, which is dead configuration, or Ok with a real 10 s deadline in force, is third-party library behaviour absent from this repository. The swallow at ipc/lib.rs:189 and the assertion at :423 are both satisfied by either outcome, so source alone cannot establish that no deadline is installed. The doc comment at :172 is the only in-repo support and is unverified prose.

validation_plan.local: Owner-run, bounded, one connection, no stress and no saturation, and explicitly NOT re-testing the daemon escalation, which belongs to the other record. Fact A, the decisive question, whether a deadline is actually in force on this platform: bind a listener, connect one client, accept it, and from the client write zero bytes; measure the elapsed time of one server-side read_frame. Refuting outcome, read_frame returns before IO_TIMEOUT with a timed-out error, which would mean a deadline IS installed and this record does not manifest on the tested platform. Confirming outcome, the read is still blocked well past 10 s under a hard 60 s cap, which means no deadline is in force. Close the handle immediately afterwards. Fact B, symmetric check for the send path: have a client that sends a complete frame and then stops reading, and measure whether the server's write_frame returns promptly or blocks. Do not attempt to drive a reply larger than the OS pipe buffer on this unauthenticated path, because the responses there are small and the write trigger was refuted from source. Control, required before trusting either result: a client that writes a complete frame plus a newline must be served normally, proving the harness works and the observation is about the stall. Regression case for any fix: assert that a reader that never sends a newline is released within IO_TIMEOUT and that a stalled writer is released symmetrically. On Windows the mechanism cannot be a receive timeout, so a watchdog that cancels or closes the handle after IO_TIMEOUT is the plausible design and must be checked not to race the worker's own use of the same Stream at main.rs:177-194. Stop after the first confirmed or refuting observation.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed read only, no probe of a live target. Record which platform the daemon is actually deployed on: on Unix a receive timeout maps to SO_RCVTIMEO and the read is bounded at IO_TIMEOUT, so this record does not manifest there, and the e2e harness is Windows-only. Also record whether any installation runs more than one identity concurrently through a single daemon, since that is what makes the fixed pool and the board mutex shared resources rather than per-invocation ones. Nothing outside the repository can bound an in-process deadline.

title: Unbounded, unescaped Envelope strings reach the daemon's rejection log through every !ok path, including both pre-cryptography branches
description: Principal 1 is any local process on the machine, unauthenticated, which the architecture summary already lists as the lowest-trust principal and which the design deliberately admits has no credential at the transport hop. It sends one newline-delimited JSON frame of at most MAX_FRAME_BYTES, 1 MiB, on the daemon named pipe. The framing and decode boundary applies only a whole-frame size check (ipc/lib.rs:224, :233); Envelope.sender_id (envelope.rs:119) and Envelope.channel (envelope.rs:125) are bare String fields with no serde length bound, so a single frame admits up to about 1 MiB of attacker-chosen UTF-8 in either field, including 0x0D 0x0A and 0x1B. The charset and length controls that exist, validate_identity at ids.rs:44 and validate_channel at ids.rs:73, are wired only into Envelope::validate (envelope.rs:258), which is reached only from verify_with_key (keys.rs:282). Board::dispatch rejects at the version branch (idboardd/src/lib.rs:95) and the registration branch (:105) before any cryptography, and every !ok response is rendered by rejection_line (idboardd/src/lib.rs:242-252) with Display formatting at lines 246-247 and emitted to the operator's stderr at main.rs:183-186. CORRECTION to the original candidate's trace: the sink is reached on every !ok response, not only the two pre-authentication branches. A peer that holds any registered key can also sign an envelope whose channel contains control characters, have verify_with_key reject it at keys.rs:282 with a bad-request error, and reach the same unescaped interpolation; that principal is a same-user process, which the design places inside the documented boundary, so it adds no cross-boundary reach. Because Display on a Rust str performs no escaping, an embedded CR/LF becomes a real line break and one request emits several lines shaped like genuine rejections, for example a forged line naming another identity as the claimed sender on a restricted channel, and terminal escape sequences in the same fields reach the operator's console. The stop point is the daemon's rejection log, which README and AGENTS.md name as the post-incident attribution record; no board state, key, or message body is affected and no identity gains authority. The impact is therefore audit-trail integrity for the operator and for any agent that greps that log, not privilege gain across a boundary. Smallest fix, enforced at the last trusted decision point: escape at the render, in rejection_line, rather than at the wire boundary, by formatting sender_id and channel with a debug formatter as the UnknownIdentity detail already does at idboardd/src/lib.rs:107-113, and by bounding each to a fixed prefix. The defence-in-depth complement is to apply validate_identity and validate_channel in Board::dispatch before the version and registration branches, which is where the invariant belongs, rather than relying on a later check.
claimed_root_cause: The framing and decode boundary imposes no per-field length or charset bound on Envelope's string fields, and the one consumer that renders a rejected envelope for every !ok response formats sender_id and channel with Display instead of an escaping formatter, so the charset controls that exist in ids.rs are unreachable on the rejection path.

trace.scope: daemon named pipe, principal 1: any local process, unauthenticated, no token and no peer credential
trace.description: read_frame_from loops on reader.fill_buf() at line 210 and returns to decode_frame at line 229 once a newline is found at line 222. The only size control applied before the decode is the whole-frame check at line 224; MAX_FRAME_BYTES is 1 MiB at line 39. No per-field bound is applied to any decoded string.

trace.scope: serde_json::from_slice::<DaemonRequest>
trace.description: decode_frame materialises DaemonRequest. Envelope.sender_id (crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:119) and Envelope.channel (envelope.rs:125) are bare String fields with no declared maximum and no serde length attribute, so both may carry up to about 1 MiB of attacker-chosen UTF-8 including 0x0D 0x0A and ESC inside one frame.

trace.scope: Board::dispatch version branch, pre-cryptography, no key required
trace.description: A mismatched req.v is rejected here and an unregistered sender_id at line 105, both before verify_with_key at line 116 and therefore reachable by a peer holding no key. Both produce an error response, so the response is not ok. A peer that does hold a registered key reaches the same !ok state via the validate call at crates/idboard-core/src/keys.rs:282.

trace.scope: idboardd::serve, holding the global board mutex taken at main.rs:135
trace.description: serve inspects the response at line 180 and, for every rejection, calls rejection_line with the raw request envelope at lines 185-186. The validated copy is not substituted, and the test at crates/idboardd/src/lib.rs:632-652 pins the same unescaped format.

trace.scope: operator stderr, via the eprintln at crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:183-186; the only production caller of rejection_line
trace.description: rejection_line interpolates env.sender_id at line 246 and env.channel.as_str() at line 247 with Display formatting, which performs no escaping of CR, LF or ESC. One request can therefore forge additional log lines in the exact shape the operator relies on for attribution, or emit terminal control sequences into the operator's console.

evidence.description: The whole-frame check `if buf.len() + i > MAX_FRAME_BYTES` is the only size control before the decode; the parallel check at line 233 covers the no-newline branch. Nothing narrows it per field.
`pub sender_id: String` with no serde length attribute and no declaration-level bound. Line 125 is the same for `pub channel: String`.

validate_identity rejects control characters and anything over 64 bytes; validate_channel at line 73 does the same for 128 bytes. Both exist and both are reachable only through Envelope::validate at envelope.rs:258, which is called from LocalSigner::finish (keys.rs:209) and from verify_with_key (keys.rs:282).

The UnknownIdentity branch formats sender_id with a debug formatter at lines 107-113, so the detail string is escaped; the unescaped copies are the two fields rejection_line itself adds at lines 246-247.
`env.sender_id,` inside a plain format placeholder, and line 247 `env.channel.as_str(),` inside another. Display on a Rust str does not escape control characters.
The rejection eprintln runs for every not-ok response, so all three rejection branches reach the sink, not only the two pre-authentication ones.

rejection_lines_are_greppable_and_name_the_claim asserts the format only on benign ASCII values, so no regression case pins behaviour for embedded control characters and any fix must keep this test green.

ListenerOptions::new().name(name).create_sync() with no security descriptor or DACL. The effective DACL of the daemon pipe is therefore the platform default and is neither set nor verified anywhere in the tree, which is why cross-account reachability is a deployment fact rather than a source fact.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox available on the audit host to execute the bounded local check

the effective DACL of the daemon named pipe is never set or verified by this code, because bind uses a bare ListenerOptions at ipc/lib.rs:108, so whether a cross-account principal can open the pipe is not source-visible; same-user reachability is source-established

how a given terminal emulator renders the injected escape bytes is a property of that emulator, not of this repository, so the console-repaint half of the claimed impact is established by reading the render call rather than observed

validation_plan.local: On an isolated Windows host with a scratch state root: build the workspace, then run the daemon with explicit config, socket and db paths and with stderr redirected to a file. From a separate unprivileged process open the pipe and write exactly one line, no raw newline inside the JSON structure, terminated by a single newline, total under 1 MiB, whose sender_id contains a JSON-escaped carriage-return/newline pair followed by a forged rejection-shaped line. Expectation: the daemon replies not-ok with a bad-request error from the version branch, and the stderr file grows by two or more lines rather than one, the second matching the rejection shape and carrying the injected claimed sender. Repeat with v=1 and an unregistered sender_id to exercise the registration branch, and repeat ten times to assert the line count grows by at least 20 for ten requests. Control: the same ten requests with a single-character sender_id must grow the file by exactly ten lines. Third case: a signed envelope from a registered key whose channel contains a newline, to confirm the verify_with_key rejection path at keys.rs:282 reaches the same sink.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed read: have the operator record the security descriptor of the daemon named pipe and note who may open it for read and write. If only the creating account and SYSTEM are granted, the affected principal is same-user and the result is audit-trail integrity for the operator; if a broader group is granted, it extends to cross-account log forgery. Neither fact is visible in this repository.

title: Store::open creates the state root holding idboard.db with the permissive directory helper, while the keystore and relay directories in the same root use the owner-only helper
description: Starting principal: a local account other than the one running the daemon, on a host where the state root is created by this code rather than pre-created by the operator. Starting capability: read access to the state directory. Accepted action: none from a peer; the relevant event is directory and file creation at daemon startup. The protected resource is idboard.db, whose messages table (store/lib.rs:78-88) holds every message body and channel, whose identities table (:96-103) holds every identity name, role, public key, fingerprint and last_seq, and whose WAL sidecars hold the same content. The control the rest of the tree relies on is owner-only creation of the state root: ensure_private_dir applies mode 0o700 under #[cfg(unix)] (layout.rs:169-173) and the crate documentation states the rationale at layout.rs:161-166. Store::open does not use it; at store/lib.rs:114-116 it calls idboard_core::layout::ensure_dir, a bare create_dir_all (layout.rs:157-159), and then opens the database at :118 inside that directory. Three sibling call sites exist: keystore.rs:112 and wrapper.rs:227 take the stricter ensure_private_dir path, while lock.rs:60 takes the permissive one, so the divergence is between call sites inside one state root, not between crates with different policies. MATERIAL BOUND THE ORIGINAL CANDIDATE UNDERSTATED: on the project's primary platform the two helpers are behaviourally identical, because ensure_private_dir's only added action is inside #[cfg(unix)] and its non-unix arm is `let _ = dir;` (layout.rs:174-177). The divergence therefore has no effect on Windows at all, where confidentiality of the database already rests entirely on the inherited NTFS ACL that this code neither sets nor verifies. The finding is a Unix-only hardening gap, and on Unix its size is set by the process umask and by the SQLite library default for a newly created file, neither of which is visible in this repository's source. What the source does establish is the divergence itself, and that it is applied per-subdirectory and never to the root, so the file carrying the message bodies receives the permissive treatment while the directory carrying the seeds does not.
claimed_root_cause: Store::open calls layout::ensure_dir, a bare create_dir_all, for the parent of idboard.db at crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs:115, while Keystore::save_seed (crates/idboard/src/keystore.rs:112) and wrapper::run_child (crates/idboard/src/wrapper.rs:227) call layout::ensure_private_dir for subdirectories of the same state root and IdentityLock::try_acquire_at (crates/idboard/src/lock.rs:60) calls the permissive helper again, so no code path ever restricts the directory that holds the database.

trace.scope: daemon startup
trace.description: Store::open(path) takes the parent of the database path, which resolves through layout::db_path() to the state root's idboard.db (crates/idboard-core/src/layout.rs:89-90). This is reached from idboardd/src/main.rs:83 on every daemon start and, because the check branch is evaluated after it, from the --check flag at idboardd/src/main.rs:95 as well.

trace.scope: daemon startup
trace.description: The parent is created with idboard_core::layout::ensure_dir, which is std::fs::create_dir_all and nothing else (crates/idboard-core/src/layout.rs:157-159). The ensure_private_dir variant that would apply 0o700 under #[cfg(unix)] is available and is not called here.

trace.scope: the protected resource itself
trace.description: Connection::open(path) creates idboard.db inside that directory with whatever mode the platform and the SQLite library default yield, and the WAL pragma at line 131 configures the same connection's journal mode. Those files carry the messages and identities tables.

evidence.description: pub fn ensure_dir(dir: &Path) is exactly std::fs::create_dir_all(dir). No permission is set, on any platform.

ensure_private_dir is ensure_dir plus set_permissions(0o700) under #[cfg(unix)] at lines 169-173, and a no-op on Windows at lines 174-177. Its doc comment at lines 161-166 states the intent: owner-only, because NTFS inheritance is relied on for Windows. This is the fact that bounds the finding: the two helpers are indistinguishable on the primary platform.

The keystore directory, a sibling of the database inside the same state root, does call layout::ensure_private_dir. The divergence is therefore between two call sites in one root, not between two crates with different policies.
ensure_private_dir on the run directory creates the state root by way of create_dir_all and then restricts only run/, leaving the parent at the permissive default. A third call site, same divergence.

ADDED BY REVIEW: IdentityLock::try_acquire_at also calls layout::ensure_dir for the run directory's parent. On a daemon-only host that never runs a wrapper, run/ is therefore created at the permissive default and never subsequently restricted. A fourth call site, and it strengthens the divergence.

The WAL journal_mode pragma. That the database's WAL and shared-memory sidecars are created in the database's own parent directory is documented SQLite behaviour rather than a fact this repository's source establishes; it is recorded as a blocker.

The messages table at lines 78-88 stores body, channel and sender_id text; the identities table at lines 96-103 stores name, role, pubkey, fingerprint, last_seq and last_seen_ms. These are the resources the divergence would expose.

Store::open is the only production constructor; open_in_memory at line 123 is test-only. There is no other place in the tree that creates or restricts the state root, so this single call site is the whole of the control.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox available on the audit host to execute the bounded local check
the mode std::fs::create_dir_all produces is the platform default filtered by the process umask, which is not recorded in this repository's source
the mode SQLite/rusqlite uses when Connection::open creates a new database file is a third-party library default, not visible in this repository's source
that SQLite's WAL and shared-memory sidecars are created in the database's parent directory is documented library behaviour rather than a source fact in this repository

on the project's primary platform the divergence has no observable effect at all, because ensure_private_dir is behaviourally identical to ensure_dir there (crates/idboard-core/src/layout.rs:174-177); only a Unix deployment can manifest it

validation_plan.local: Owner-run on a Unix host, in a scratch state root with a known umask: set a known umask, run the daemon's --check flag, which reaches Store::open at crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs:113 via crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:83 and :95. Then stat the state root and the database and compare against the keys directory. The expected finding is that the state root and the database are less restrictive than the keystore directory. The smallest source change is to call ensure_private_dir(parent) at crates/idboard-store/src/lib.rs:115 instead of ensure_dir, and to use the same helper at crates/idboard/src/lock.rs:60; a stronger variant additionally opens the database with an explicit owner-only mode, since directory mode alone does not constrain an already-existing file.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed read on the real host: after starting the daemon, list the permissions and ACLs of the state root, the keys directory and the database files and confirm whether the intended account is the only principal with read access to the database and its sidecars. If the deployment is Windows only, record that the code path is the non-unix no-op at crates/idboard-core/src/layout.rs:174-177, that the divergence therefore has no effect there, and that confidentiality rests entirely on the inherited NTFS ACL, which this repository neither sets nor verifies.

title: The read projection omits the persisted channel column and substitutes an empty one, so a message read back from the board is not the envelope that was authenticated and cannot be re-verified
description: Starting capability: any identity the config authorises to read a channel, that is, a child agent holding its wrapper's relay token, or any same-user process holding that identity's key. Accepted action: read on a channel the caller is legitimately allowed to read. State transition: none on the write side; the read side projects stored rows into a StoredMessage and hands it to the caller. The strongest source-visible control that should bind the disclosed value to the authenticated one is the ed25519 signature over the canonical bytes, which covers channel among its nine fields (SignedFields at envelope.rs:145-155, channel serialised at envelope.rs:212). The control actually applied on the read side is only a channel equality predicate in the WHERE clause, which selects rows but does not carry the channel into the reconstructed value. Store::read selects cursor, sender_id, sender_fp, seq, provenance, body, ts_ms and the lowercased hex signature at store/lib.rs:275 and omits channel, even though channel is both the predicate at :277 and a persisted column written from the authenticated envelope at :239. row_to_message then hardcodes an empty channel at :357, alongside a fixed op at :354 and an empty nonce at :362, so the envelope a reader receives is not the envelope that was verified. Two corrections to the original candidate. First, the signature field is serialised with put_u16, not put_u32, at envelope.rs:212; the conclusion that channel is unconditionally inside the signed byte string, with no op-dependent omission, is unchanged. Second, re-verification fails earlier than the candidate states: verify_with_key calls env.validate() at keys.rs:282 before it ever builds canonical bytes, and for a post the op invariants call validate_channel on that channel at envelope.rs:286, which rejects the empty string at ids.rs:74-76 with a bad-request error. The empty nonce is consistent for a post and is not itself a divergence. The reconstruction therefore cannot be re-verified, and it fails closed. Containment, established and not overstated: no cross-channel disclosure occurs. The row filter is parameterised (store/lib.rs:281), the ACL is checked against the verified identity at idboardd/src/lib.rs:203 before the query at :209, and the stored sender_id is bound from the config-derived verified name at store/lib.rs:240 rather than from the envelope, so a reader still sees only rows from the channel it was authorised for and cannot forge a sender by reading. VERIFIED: no code in the tree re-verifies a read-back StoredMessage; the only production call to verify_with_key is idboardd/src/lib.rs:116 and the remaining hits are unit tests. So the impact is confined to two things: the JSON read path publishes an empty channel field for every message because StoredMessage flattens the envelope onto the wire (wire.rs:21-22, printed at cli.rs:165), and the board's read output cannot be checked against the signature that produced it. That is an integrity and auditability defect in a system whose stated value is that the signature tells the reader who said it; it is not a forgery primitive, and no identity gains authority. The divergence is specific to the read projection: handle_post returns the full cloned envelope at store/lib.rs:253, so a poster sees its own channel intact in the post reply while a reader does not.
claimed_root_cause: The SELECT projection in Store::read omits the persisted channel column (store/lib.rs:275) and row_to_message substitutes a constant for it (:357, alongside a fixed op at :354 and an empty nonce at :362), so the StoredMessage returned to a reader does not carry the field the ed25519 signature covers, and no downstream consumer re-verifies stored messages to notice.

trace.scope: handle_read, reached only with a verified identity and a passed ACL
trace.description: handle_read calls store.read on the signed, ACL-checked channel after the skew check at line 202 and authorize at line 203. That channel is the only channel selector that reaches storage.

trace.scope: the cached statement's SELECT list
trace.description: The projection is cursor, sender_id, sender_fp, seq, provenance, body, ts_ms and the lowercased hex signature. channel is used as the WHERE predicate at line 277 and is written on insert at line 239, but it is not projected, so the column's value is discarded at the moment the row crosses into a value type.

trace.scope: the value handed back to the reader
trace.description: row_to_message builds an Envelope with a fixed op, an empty channel and an empty nonce at lines 353-364. This StoredMessage is returned to handle_read and serialised to the caller with the envelope flattened (crates/idboard-core/src/wire.rs:21-22), so the reader receives a value whose channel is empty and whose canonical bytes cannot match the signed bytes.

evidence.description: put_u16 on the channel inside SignedFields::to_canonical_bytes: channel is unconditionally part of the signed byte string, with no op-dependent omission. CORRECTION: the original candidate cited put_u32 here; the call at this line is put_u16, with put_u32 used for sender_pubkey_fp at :211, body at :213 and nonce at :216.

CORRECTION to the original candidate's failure mechanism: verify_with_key calls env.validate as its first statement, before hex-decoding the signature at :284 and before verify_strict at :298. For a post the op invariants call validate_channel on that channel at crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:286, which rejects the empty string at crates/idboard-core/src/ids.rs:74-76. Re-verification therefore fails at structural validation, not at verify_strict, and it fails closed.
The INSERT binds envelope.channel as column 1, so the authenticated channel IS persisted. The information needed for the reader exists in the row and is simply not read back.
handle_post's reply carries the full original cloned envelope. The divergence is therefore specific to the read projection, not to the value type.

The comment states that without lowercasing a read-back signature would not compare equal to the one that was signed, which would silently break any re-verification against stored data. The premise is contradicted by the omitted channel column, so the documented intent of the projection is not met by the projection.

append_and_read_round_trip asserts body, sender_id, seq, provenance and signature but never asserts the read-back channel and never calls a verify helper on the result, so no test in the suite would fail on this. The board-level tests assert bodies and senders, never the read-back channel.

A serde flatten attribute on line 21 applies to the envelope field on line 22, so the empty channel is published verbatim on the wire rather than hidden behind a projection type, and appears as an empty channel field in the JSON read output printed at crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:165.

The only production call to verify_with_key in the workspace. A workspace-wide search returns this call, two re-exports, and unit tests only; no consumer re-verifies a message after it has been through the read projection.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox available on the audit host to execute the bounded local check

whether any consumer depends on the read-back channel field or attempts re-verification of board output is not observable from this repository: no code in the tree reads envelope.channel off a StoredMessage, and the text renderer at crates/idboard/src/cli.rs:173 and :214 uses only sender_id, cursor, provenance and body. The empty field is therefore visible only through the JSON path, and the operational consequence of that is a deployment fact.

validation_plan.local: Owner-run, in crates/idboard-store: add a test that registers a signer, appends a post to a channel, reads it back, and asserts both that the read-back channel equals the original and that re-verification against the signer's public key succeeds. Both assertions must fail on the current source, the first with an empty channel at store/lib.rs:357 and the second with a bad-request error from validate_channel at crates/idboard-core/src/envelope.rs:286; both must pass once channel is added to the projection at store/lib.rs:275 and read from the row instead of being hardcoded. The smallest source change is to add channel to the SELECT list and pass the row value into the envelope. The fixed op and empty nonce may stay, because a post with an empty nonce is the correct shape for the only thing append ever persists, and because the nonce is signed as empty for every post the wrapper produces.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed read: run the JSON read form against a scratch board that already holds a message and observe an empty channel field on every returned message, alongside the correct body, sender_id and seq. This is a display confirmation only and requires no board mutation.

title: The single process-wide Board mutex is acquired before the peer-paced read, so one stalled unauthenticated pipe connection holds the board for every identity
description: Verified mechanism, with the impact tightened. Principal 1 is any local process that can open the daemon named pipe; bind installs no DACL (ipc/lib.rs:108) and accept installs no credential, so authentication happens only later at idboardd/src/lib.rs:116 and an unauthenticated peer is fully reachable. The peer connects, sends zero bytes, and holds the handle. A worker has already taken the one board mutex (main.rs:117) at main.rs:135 before any byte is read, and passes the still-live guard to serve at main.rs:139, so the global lock is held across the blocking read at main.rs:177. Every subsequent connection from any other identity is picked up by another worker that blocks on the same mutex at main.rs:135, so the victim's signed post, read or handshake is never dispatched. The affected principal is genuinely a DIFFERENT identity, not the stalling client: the shared resource is the single in-process board mutex, and the victim's request is refused service because a second, unrelated process holds that lock. Corrections to the original candidate. (a) Impact scaling: the cross-identity effect begins with the FIRST legitimate connection from any other identity, because that connection's worker blocks on board.lock(); total loss of the accept loop additionally requires the remaining three workers to be blocked and the 64-deep sync_channel (main.rs:111) to fill, that is roughly 67 further connections beyond the attacker's. The original phrasing that one connect stops the daemon accepting overstates it. (b) The write trigger as claimed is REFUTED for the unauthenticated case: every response on the pre-authentication rejection paths (main.rs:191, idboardd/src/lib.rs:96, idboardd/src/lib.rs:105) is a small bounded string, which a small write_frame (ipc/lib.rs:256-265) delivers into the OS pipe buffer, so write_all at ipc/lib.rs:262 does not block. The write path becomes a trigger only for a reply larger than the pipe buffer, which source does not establish as reachable without a key; it is demoted from sink to evidence. (c) Cost and persistence are accurate: one connect, zero crafted bytes, no key, no privilege, no rate limit anywhere in the tree, effect lasting until the attacker closes, at which point read_frame returns Ok(None) (ipc/lib.rs:215-217) and the guard drops. Controls that bound but do not prevent the result: the fixed worker count (main.rs:25) and queue depth (main.rs:29, :111) cap threads and queue depth, and MAX_FRAME_BYTES (ipc/lib.rs:39) caps bytes once they arrive, so the daemon does not exhaust memory or CPU. The failure mode is loss of the shared coordination point that the architecture summary names as a protected resource, and the documented consequence at main.rs:23 and README.md:328, that a stalled client costs throughput, omits the single global mutex that turns per-worker retention into cross-identity unavailability. This record consumes the missing-deadline precondition recorded under idboard-ipc.apply_timeouts.unsupported_swallow_removes_read_deadline; that precondition is a distinct root cause in a distinct crate and is not re-claimed here. Fix check: the proposed reordering is sound and does not move trust. Board::handle (idboardd/src/lib.rs:87) performs only bounded local work and never touches the stream, so reading the frame and writing the reply and the eprintln (main.rs:183) outside the guard while holding it only around handle preserves every security decision at the last trusted decision point. The same discipline is already applied in-tree: the wrapper deliberately never holds its sequence-number mutex across the daemon round trip (relay.rs:69), which is precisely what the daemon's board mutex does.
claimed_root_cause: The worker loop acquires the single process-wide board mutex at crates/idboardd/src/main.rs:135 and passes the live guard into serve at :139, so the one shared serialisation point covers the entire peer-paced, deadline-free read at :177 and write at :194 instead of only the bounded board mutation inside Board::handle.

trace.scope: unauthenticated local process: no token, no DACL, no peer credential, key not yet required
trace.description: idboard_ipc::accept(&listener) returns a Stream to any local process that opens the daemon named pipe. bind used a bare ListenerOptions construction (ipc/lib.rs:108), so no security descriptor restricts the opener, and accept applies only apply_timeouts (ipc/lib.rs:137), which is a no-op on the primary platform.

trace.scope: accept loop, main thread
trace.description: tx.send hands the connection to the 64-deep sync_channel created at main.rs:111. This is the only queue bound in the daemon and it blocks the accept loop once full, which is what converts per-worker retention into loss of accept.

trace.scope: worker thread, one of the four spawned at main.rs:120-123
trace.description: board.lock() is taken on the single board mutex created at main.rs:117, before a single byte has been read from the peer. The PoisonError arm at main.rs:137 recovers via into_inner, so this is the ordinary path, not an error path.

trace.scope: worker thread
trace.description: serve takes the guard by mutable borrow, so the global board lock is held for the whole of serve (main.rs:168-196). Each of the other three workers, as it takes its own connection, then blocks on the same mutex at main.rs:135.

trace.scope: peer-paced blocking read executed while the global board mutex is held
trace.description: idboard_ipc::read_frame blocks in BufRead::fill_buf at ipc/lib.rs:210 until a newline, EOF or error. No deadline is installed on the accepted stream because apply_timeouts discards ErrorKind::Unsupported and returns Ok (ipc/lib.rs:189, :193), so a peer that sends nothing holds the global board mutex for as long as it keeps the handle open, and every other identity's connection queues behind that same lock.

evidence.description: The single process-wide board mutex, shared by all workers and therefore by all identities. The comment at :114-116 justifies it as optimising away a cost, and does not consider a peer-paced operation inside the guard.
The lock acquisition; this is both the defect location and the smallest-fix location, because the lock is taken before the peer read.
The guard is passed by mutable borrow, so it is alive across the read at :177, the rejection eprintln at :183 and the socket write at :194.
The bounded queue. Once the other three workers are blocked on the board mutex, queued connections accumulate here and the accept loop blocks at :148.
The fixed worker count, which combined with the single board mutex is the whole of the daemon's concurrency budget.

The documented model, that a fixed pool costs throughput, describes per-worker retention and never mentions the single board mutex taken at :135, which is what makes the consequence cross-identity rather than per-connection.

Board::handle performs bounded local work only and no stream I/O: dispatch checks version at :95, registration at :105, signature at :116, then authorizes and either appends at :188 or reads at :209. Reading the frame and writing the reply outside the guard therefore weakens no check and leaves every decision inside the lock.

The comment that the relay's sequence-number mutex is never held across the daemon round trip so a slow daemon cannot serialise unrelated posts. This is the in-repo precedent for exactly the discipline the daemon's board mutex omits: the same tree, the same class of shared mutex, applied correctly in the wrapper and incorrectly in the daemon.

The response write is inside the guard, but the write trigger as claimed is NOT established for the unauthenticated case: the pre-authentication responses (main.rs:191, idboardd/src/lib.rs:96, :105) are small and are absorbed by the OS pipe buffer, so write_all (ipc/lib.rs:262) does not block for them. The write becomes a trigger only for a reply exceeding the pipe buffer, which source does not show is reachable without a key.

The rejection eprintln is a third blocking-capable operation inside the critical section. If stderr is a slow or full sink, a shared resource stalls for every identity independently of the peer, so the fix must move this out of the guard as well.

The accepted-risk statement that a client which connects and then stalls costs throughput rather than the process. Accurate for worker slots alone; it does not account for the single board mutex, so it understates the multi-identity case.

blockers: no OS-enforced sandbox on the audit host to execute the bounded local check; the consequence of holding the lock across a peer-paced read requires observing a second identity's request being withheld, which cannot be established from source alone

the effective DACL of the daemon named pipe is never set or verified by this code, because bind uses a bare ListenerOptions construction at ipc/lib.rs:108, so whether a principal in a different OS account, as opposed to the same account, can open the pipe is not source-visible; same-user reachability is source-established and is sufficient for the mechanism

validation_plan.local: Owner-run on an isolated Windows host, one connection at a time, no saturation or concurrency stress. Scratch state root with a two-identity config, each with its own generated pubkey, one channel permitting both identities to post and read, and a fresh database; start the daemon and confirm it reports its workers ready. Phase 1, the decisive read trigger: open ONE pipe handle, write zero bytes, and keep it open with a 15-second sleep before any cleanup. While it is open, from a second process run a post as the second identity under a 30-second timeout. Confirming observations are: the stalled handle remains open, the second process returns no response, and the daemon's accept loop stops draining. Control: close the stalled handle, re-run the same post, and confirm it now succeeds, proving recovery occurs only when the attacker disconnects. Stop at the first confirmed timeout. Do NOT attempt to observe the queue saturation or open more than one concurrent stalled handle; that figure is analytic and is recorded as such, not tested. Phase 2 is unnecessary: the write trigger was refuted from source and must not be probed.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed read only, no probe of a live target. Confirm from the deployment description whether any real installation runs two or more identities concurrently through a single daemon, since that is what makes the board mutex a shared multi-tenant resource rather than a per-invocation one; and record the platform ACL on the pipe if a cross-account attacker is in scope. No autoscaling, gateway or per-tenant quota exists to bound the in-process board mutex, so nothing outside the repository can mitigate it.
